svg.title: Intellectual influences and arguments across time
svg.desc: Source-backed arrows connect earlier thinkers or proposals to later recipients or critics. Cards show representative readings and publication periods. Green means credited influence; blue dotted means explicit engagement; red dashed means criticism by the receiving author. Every numbered arrow has a linked source and a scope note.
svg.text: AI CULTURAL MOVEMENTS / AN INTELLECTUAL HISTORY
Follow arrows from an earlier thinker or proposal to the later recipient or critic. Cards give representative readings.
Shared era bands; non-linear spacing. Arrows concern authors unless the key names a specific text. A citation alone is not classified as formative influence.

a.title: 1. Plato → Aristotle: teacher and interlocutor. Author-level relationship; Meno and Nicomachean Ethics are representative readings, not a claim that one directly produced the other.
2. Aristotle → Bacon: replaces the old Organon. Novum Organum explicitly challenges the inherited syllogistic method; see Book I and the editorial introduction.
3. Aristotle → Boole: algebraizes syllogisms. Boole treats Aristotelian syllogistic in Laws of Thought, chapter XV. This is explicit formal reworking, not a claim of personal inspiration.
4. Descartes → Hume: limits of radical doubt. Enquiry section XII explicitly discusses and criticizes Cartesian antecedent skepticism.
5. Bacon → Bentham: empirical method. Author-level influence explicitly identified in the scholarly account of Bentham’s intellectual development.
6. Hume → Bentham: utility. Bentham credits Hume’s Treatise, rather than the Enquiry displayed here, with his turn toward utility. This is an author-level edge.
7. Bentham → Mill: formative utilitarianism. Mill’s autobiographical account credits Bentham’s ideas; Mill later revised the doctrine.
8. Mill → Sidgwick: develops and revises. The Methods develops classical utilitarianism in response to Bentham and Mill.
9. Sidgwick → Singer: acknowledged influence. Author-level influence on Singer’s ethical thought, not a claim that the 1972 essay is a direct adaptation of The Methods.
10. Sidgwick → Parfit: acknowledged influence. Parfit acknowledges The Methods as a source; population ethics develops questions raised by Sidgwick.
11. Singer → MacAskill: formative encounter. MacAskill credits an undergraduate encounter with Singer’s argument with reshaping his life; the target is the author represented by Doing Good Better.
12. Singer → Ord: ethical inspiration. Author-level influence on Ord’s altruism, not a claim that The Precipice directly derives from this essay.
13. Parfit → Ord: mentor. Ord studied under Parfit and describes him as a mentor.

14. Parfit → MacAskill: mentor. MacAskill’s coauthored Moral Uncertainty is dedicated to Parfit as mentor and friend; this is an author-level relationship, not an assertion about a specific borrowed passage.

15. Bayes → Jaynes: explicitly discusses. Probability Theory §4.6.1 discusses Bayes’s 1763 result and distinguishes it from Laplace’s broader contribution. This is textual reception, not a complete Bayesian genealogy.
16. Jaynes → Yudkowsky: credited turning point. In My Bayesian Enlightenment, Yudkowsky explicitly credits Probability Theory with changing his approach.

17. Hofstadter → Yudkowsky: formative model. Yudkowsky identifies Hofstadter as a childhood hero; his account also records disagreement about intelligence. The arrow is not an endorsement of Yudkowsky by Hofstadter.
18. Kahneman / Tversky → Yudkowsky: applies. The collection’s introduction explicitly builds its account of biases around Tversky and Kahneman’s findings; individual essays also cite this research.

19. Simon → Kahneman: bounded rationality. Kahneman explicitly discusses Simon’s bounded-rationality framework in his 2002 Nobel lecture. Author-level reception evidenced in 2002, not proof that the displayed 1982 anthology derives from Simon’s 1969 book.
20. Simon → Dreyfus: symbolic-AI critique. Dreyfus’s own 1974 exchange, defending What Computers Can’t Do, explicitly challenges Simon’s claims about AI progress.

21. Turing test → Searle: understanding objection. Minds, Brains, and Programs argues that passing a Turing test is insufficient for understanding. Its immediate target is strong-AI claims, not every claim in Turing’s paper.

22. I. J. Good → Bostrom: intelligence explosion. Bostrom explicitly quotes and develops Good’s 1965 argument in his work on humanity’s future; author-level reception predating the displayed 2014 book.

23. I. J. Good → Yudkowsky: intelligence explosion. Bostrom and Yudkowsky’s coauthored The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence explicitly presents Good’s classic hypothesis. Evidence is the later coauthored paper, not the displayed Sequences collection itself.

24. Moravec → Bostrom: computational estimates. Bostrom’s How Long Before Superintelligence? explicitly discusses Moravec’s estimates. Author-level engagement, not agreement with every claim in Mind Children.

25. Russell → Christian: research chronicled. CHAI reports that The Alignment Problem showcases Stuart Russell’s research; the link is to the research, not a claim that Human Compatible caused Christian’s book.

26. Kurzweil → Andreessen: named inspiration. Andreessen explicitly includes Kurzweil in the manifesto’s list of intellectual inspirations. Author-level acknowledgment; it does not identify a specific Kurzweil book.
27. Deutsch → Andreessen: quoted and credited. The manifesto quotes Deutsch and lists him among its intellectual inspirations; The Beginning of Infinity is a representative reading.
28. MacAskill → Srinivasan: direct critical review. Stop the Robot Apocalypse directly reviews Doing Good Better and questions EA’s treatment of politics and systemic change.

svg.text: Reading dates locate the displayed works. Some author-level evidence comes from other works or later recollections; full scope notes are in the source ledger.
The former thematic bridges and automatic reading-order chains have been removed. Source links are embedded in arrows, number badges, and the evidence key.
